newsitem.title: USA: Floods, fire, evacuation at stricken N.Dakota city. [CORRECTED 19:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Floods, fire, evacuation at stricken N.Dakota city. [CORRECTED 19:00 GMT]

text.p: The swollen Red River advanced relentlessly over this flood-stricken and fire-ravaged North Dakota city on Monday and emergency officials warned that more disaster could lie ahead.

Hospital patients and high-risk federal prisoners joined an exodus of thousands of refugees from Grand Forks, where dark, icy floodwaters swirled waist-deep through a downtown left partially gutted and ghostly by fire.

President Bill Clinton announced plans to visit the stricken area on Tuesday for what will probably be an aerial tour and a visit with officials and residents. White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Clinton had been getting "regular updates ... (it's) obviously a very difficult situation."
A back-up power generator was moved to an ammonia plant near Grand Forks on Monday to keep the chemical cool and prevent an emergency release of poisonous fumes should power fail.

Officials said they forcibly removed two residents from homes in downtown Grand Forks (corrects from Grand Rapids) during the night. Three houses caught fire in the flood zone but the blazes were put out.

Authorities widened the mandatory evacuation zone to cover 90 percent of the city's approximately 50,000 residents. Across the river in East Grand Forks, Minnesota, the entire population was under orders to leave.
"There's always a potential for a larger area of the city to be flooded. The river is still rising," Grand Forks Emergency Manager Jim Campbell said.

Its tribulations began when the Red River punched through clay dikes and swept into the city this weekend. A devastating fire followed, searing the downtown business district as several feet of water kept firefighters away.

The last of 60 patients were evacuated late on Sunday from a hospital shut down because of advancing waters that had already forced thousands of local residents to flee. Officials also disclosed that 70 prisoners had been evacuated, including 12 high-risk federal prisoners who were taken to Devils Lake, about 90 miles (144 km) west.

Residents may not be allowed to return to their homes for more than two weeks because of the lack of services. The city's water treatment plant was flooded on Saturday and it may be three weeks before fresh water flows again.

Stunned officials spoke of the pain of seeing their city hit not only by flood but also by a fire that destroyed at least 11 buildings in the downtown area. The blaze was first reported on Saturday afternoon but was not tamed until Sunday.

Water proved to be the biggest enemy in fighting the blaze. Firefighters searched frantically through murky brown floodwaters for hydrants to which they could attach hoses, only to find no pressure in the city's water system.

They eventually gained the edge by using the floodwater itself as a weapon. In desperation, they loaded a pumper truck onto the back of a trailer and then shot floodwaters through the pumper's turret gun. Helicopters also dumped thousands of gallons (litres) of water on the blaze.

As dawn broke Monday the heart of Grand Forks lay blackened and in ruins, while in residential areas floodwaters continued to pour through schools, libraries and houses of the city's once-tidy neighborhoods.

"It was hard for me to see friends' houses down there. Some of them had not only gone under water but had collapsed. The foundation obviously had given away and was laying at a 45 or 50 degree angle," Lt. Byron Sieber, Grand Forks Emergency Operations spokesman, said about one city neighborhood overpowered by the river.

About 75 miles upstream, Fargo Mayor Bruce Furness said he was optimistic because the Red River was receding at a rate of about an inch an hour. The Red was measured at 38.74 feet Monday, down more than six inches from the week's crest level.
"We need to have two or three good days before we are going to breathe any easier. The dikes are tired, the people are tired," Furness said.
But the Red was still rising in Grand Forks, where officials expected it to crest at 54 feet -- 26 feet above flood stage.
